title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team does it for a city you haven’t modeled: Chicago.
The Cook County Assessor’s Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn’t sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they’re wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 Chicago Tribune investigation, “The Tax Divide,” found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones.
Build a model that predicts single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025, using only the tools from this course. The file contains only features of the house itself. Everything about location is yours to build.









File
What’s in it




chicago_train.csv
About 80% of the houses, with sale prices


chicago_test.csv
The other 20%, without sale prices. You predict them; we score you.



The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. If they’re far apart, something leaked.
Due: Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads team_XX_predictions.csv.
Individual accountability: Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about this model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of it.

Transform predictors, not sale_price.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
Part 1: Clean and explore
Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price.
In building our model, we only included homes price/sqft below the 0.1st percentile ($11.70/sqft). Extreme values below this cutoff point appeared to be off-market sales; a lot of larger homes sold for less than expected under ~ $15/sqft, which suggested they weren’t representative/good training observations. We removed 24 training observations due to this reason. On the other end of the spectrum, we removed homes where price/sqft was above the 99.9th percentile ($1300/sqft). Extreme values above this cutoff point were mostly multi-parcel sales which seemed to reflect the price of the full sale vs. the individual home (e.g., $21.8 million on a 2000 square foot house). This removed 24 training observations.
Lastly, one sale had no census tract match because it was located outside of ACS tract boundaries and had no associated ACS values. Because of this, we removed 1 training observation.
In total, we removed 49 observations. We used price/sqft to try to normalize the metric across home sizes/types. A lot of very expensive (high price/sqft) homes at the high end seemed to be actual sales, possibly more historic homes in more expensive parts of the city.
The four plots will be displayed below the variable data cleaning code.

What helped most, and what disappointed you? Use your log.
The most helpful improvements came from ACS socioeconomic variables, neighborhood fixed effects, and interaction between building size and neighborhood.
Adding ACS variables reduced RMSE by $47,385, neighborhood fixed effects reduced it by $24,827 and lowered Moran’s I from 0.3523 to 0.2149. The interaction between building area and neighborhood also made a big difference by reducing RMSE by $19,732.

section: Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays
text:
Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays
Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?
Based on the plots above, the model fails the most in the southern part of Chicago, specifically Roseland and South Shore. There are not uniform patterns of guessing too high or too low, rather there is a mix of patterns of overprediction and underprediction. This could be attributed to the fact that there are variables that move in conflicting directions within this region. For example, while the southern part of Chicago may have lower income rates and higher vacancy rates compared to the rest of the city, it is also closer to the lake, the loop, schools, and may have higher amounts of college-educated individuals due to proximity to universities. Thus, because of these conflicting indicators of home price coexisting in one area it may lead to more extreme over- or under-predictions that cannot be uniformly accounted for.
Assessors judge their work with the ratio of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model’s ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to “The Tax Divide.”
Based on the ratio of predicted values to sale prices, it seems that homes in the south part of Chicago are over-valued and their owners are over-taxed in comparison to other areas, possibly in part due to the reasons described above. In the initial cleaning stages of our model creation we removed homes that were above the 99.9th percentile in sales price and homes that were below the 0.1th percentile in sales price. This translates to homes that are relatively higher in sales price being under-predicted and homes that are relatively lower in sales prices being over-predicted due to the constrained range of training data. Furthermore, this connects to “The Tax Divide” which exposed how many lower-income households’ homes in Chicago were over-assessed relative to commercial and high-end residential properties. Comparing the two maps that show the ratio of predicted values to sale prices and median income, the model mirrors the same systematic biases present in Cook County’s property tax assessments in which housing in lower-income areas is over-predicted.

text:
Part 6: Reflection
Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Looking at the coefficient building_000sf β̂ represents the estimated change in sale price associated with a one-unit increase in building size. This is of course assuming that other predictors are held constant. Since building_000sf measures size in thousands of square feet, one unit represents an additional 1,000 square feet. Ŷ is the predicted sale price and so increasing building size by 1,000 square feet changes the prediction according to the coefficient. Since the final model includes a squared building-size term as well as an interaction between square footage and neighborhood, the actual effect β̂ has on ŷ, depends on the properties size and neighborhood.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?
We would not hand this model to the Assessor currently, with the high level of uncertainty in its prediction. The characteristics and variables added to our model helped predict sales price as much as possible while using open data. However, it’s crucial to recognize the major limitations inherent in our model. This model is trained on properties sold between 2023 and 2025, which does not represent all properties. Since we used median inputs for some missing property characteristics there is a chance these characteristics are skewed from the reality of the situation. We applied specific criteria to remove outliers. Therefore, the model is not trained on the complete dataset and therefore might be less accurate in predicting extremely high and low priced houses. It’s also important to note that just because a low RMSE score is achievable does not mean that prediction errors across neighborhoods and income groups don’t exist. The model and data used to feed the model could systematically under or overvalue homes in particular neighborhoods. Most importantly, our final model m15’s CV RMSE of $180,925 indicates a substantial prediction error. An error of this size could result in homeowners paying much more or less in taxes than they should. This level of uncertainty is still extraordinarily significant to be used as a prediction model. The final model would need to be significantly altered to even be considered being sent over to an Assessor.

Key Concepts
‘dplyr’ Functions

filter() // pick rows
select() // pick columns
mutate() // add new computed column
arrange() // change order of rows in ascending and descending
group_by() + summarize() // groups rows by a common function using a specific operation
case_when() // regrouping row values

Census and ACS
The Decennial Census surveys essentially the entire population in 10 years. Census geography goes in the following order:
STATE
COUNTY
TRACT (“Neighborhood” around 5,000-8,000, changing boundaries)
BLOCK GROUP (higher MOE, Decennial Census only)

The American Community Survey (ACS) became a thing in around 2005, surveying about 3% of households to provide an estimate for the larger population. The ACS previously had a survey that was conducted every 3 years, however, that no longer exists. The 1-year ACS data exists for geographic areas with more than 65,000 people. The 5-year ACS data exists at the block group and tract level. ACS data includes an estimate and a margin of error (MOE)
GEOIDs
GEOIDs are a unique gegraphic identifier code. The first two digits indicate the state, the following three indicate the county, and the last 5-6 indicate the tract.
‘tidycensus’ Functions

load_variables() // provides a codebook of variable names
get_acs() // retrieves data from Census API

variables = c(“B19013_001”, “B01003_001”),
state = “PA”,

Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 5280/2) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_intersects)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 238


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






Two different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

Part 1: Clean and explore
Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price.
In building our model, we only included homes price/sqft below the 0.1st percentile ($11.70/sqft). Extreme values below this cutoff point appeared to be off-market sales; a lot of larger homes sold for less than expected under ~ $15/sqft, which suggested they weren’t representative/good training observations. We removed 24 training observations due to this reason. On the other end of the spectrum, we removed homes where price/sqft was above the 99.9th percentile ($1300/sqft). Extreme values above this cutoff point were mostly multi-parcel sales which seemed to reflect the price of the full sale vs. the individual home (e.g., $21.8 million on a 2000 square foot house). This removed 24 training observations.
Lastly, one sale had no census tract match because it was located outside of ACS tract boundaries and had no associated ACS values. Because of this, we removed 1 training observation.
In total, we removed 49 observations. We used price/sqft to try to normalize the metric across home sizes/types. A lot of very expensive (high price/sqft) homes at the high end seemed to be actual sales, possibly more historic homes in more expensive parts of the city.
The four plots will be displayed below the variable data cleaning code.

What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Our exploration showed that sale prices depend on property characteristics and location. We included relationships between sale price and building size, age, and lot size. To account for nonlinear relationships, we tested a squared building-size term. Some property characteristics had missing values and so we filled in the missing values with the median of all of the values. We quickly found out that prices differ between neighborhoods. So, we decided to include neighborhood and census tract variables (ex. income, poverty, homeownership). Some neighborhoods had few sales and so we combined them with nearby, larger neighborhoods. We tried out different spatial variables to see if they would create any improvements (ex. Distance to transit stops, distance to schools, etc.). Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays
Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?
Based on the plots above, the model fails the most in the southern part of Chicago, specifically Roseland and South Shore. There are not uniform patterns of guessing too high or too low, rather there is a mix of patterns of overprediction and underprediction. This could be attributed to the fact that there are variables that move in conflicting directions within this region. For example, while the southern part of Chicago may have lower income rates and higher vacancy rates compared to the rest of the city, it is also closer to the lake, the loop, schools, and may have higher amounts of college-educated individuals due to proximity to universities. Thus, because of these conflicting indicators of home price coexisting in one area it may lead to more extreme over- or under-predictions that cannot be uniformly accounted for.
Assessors judge their work with the ratio of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model’s ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to “The Tax Divide.”
Based on the ratio of predicted values to sale prices, it seems that homes in the south part of Chicago are over-valued and their owners are over-taxed in comparison to other areas, possibly in part due to the reasons described above. In the initial cleaning stages of our model creation we removed homes that were above the 99.9th percentile in sales price and homes that were below the 0.1th percentile in sales price. This translates to homes that are relatively higher in sales price being under-predicted and homes that are relatively lower in sales prices being over-predicted due to the constrained range of training data. Furthermore, this connects to “The Tax Divide” which exposed how many lower-income households’ homes in Chicago were over-assessed relative to commercial and high-end residential properties. Comparing the two maps that show the ratio of predicted values to sale prices and median income, the model mirrors the same systematic biases present in Cook County’s property tax assessments in which housing in lower-income areas is over-predicted.

Part 6: Reflection
Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Looking at the coefficient building_000sf β̂ represents the estimated change in sale price associated with a one-unit increase in building size. This is of course assuming that other predictors are held constant. Since building_000sf measures size in thousands of square feet, one unit represents an additional 1,000 square feet. Ŷ is the predicted sale price and so increasing building size by 1,000 square feet changes the prediction according to the coefficient. Since the final model includes a squared building-size term as well as an interaction between square footage and neighborhood, the actual effect β̂ has on ŷ, depends on the properties size and neighborhood.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?
We would not hand this model to the Assessor currently, with the high level of uncertainty in its prediction. The characteristics and variables added to our model helped predict sales price as much as possible while using open data. However, it’s crucial to recognize the major limitations inherent in our model. This model is trained on properties sold between 2023 and 2025, which does not represent all properties. Since we used median inputs for some missing property characteristics there is a chance these characteristics are skewed from the reality of the situation. We applied specific criteria to remove outliers. Therefore, the model is not trained on the complete dataset and therefore might be less accurate in predicting extremely high and low priced houses. It’s also important to note that just because a low RMSE score is achievable does not mean that prediction errors across neighborhoods and income groups don’t exist. The model and data used to feed the model could systematically under or overvalue homes in particular neighborhoods. Most importantly, our final model m15’s CV RMSE of $180,925 indicates a substantial prediction error. An error of this size could result in homeowners paying much more or less in taxes than they should. This level of uncertainty is still extraordinarily significant to be used as a prediction model. The final model would need to be significantly altered to even be considered being sent over to an Assessor.

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.

Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?
url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=csv&q=",
              URLencode("SELECT text_general_code, COUNT(*) AS n
                         FROM incidents_part1_part2
                         WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
                         GROUP BY text_general_code ORDER BY n DESC"))

text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many bike stations fall in each tract?


Code
# check for the same coordinates #

layer1 <- st_transform(layer1, st_crs(tracts))

layer2 <- st_transform(layer2, st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_bike_stations = lengths(st_intersects(., layer2)),
         n_schools = lengths(st_intersects(., layer1)))




4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,  
    schools_per_sqmi = n_schools / area_sqmi,
    schools_per_1k   = n_schools / total_popE * 1000
  )








Per capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer2)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, layer2[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
amtrak <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.181715, 39.956634)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_amtrak_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, amtrak)) / 5280)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", 
          added = "Amtrak distance",

          notes = "Improves")

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", 
          added = "Indego station distance",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),

Based on the evidence above, it seems that distance to the William H. Gray III 30th Street Station and distance to an Indego bike station helped improve the CV RMSE the most. Conversely, the school density variable slightly worsened the CV RMSE by .01, likely because there is a looser connection to how schools translate to commute times. The initial assumption was that areas around schools may experience more morning traffic congestion; however, this may not hold in more suburban parts of Philadelphia.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






Transform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.






















log(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ n_bike_stations + I(n_bike_stations^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(

    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))

Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






Check your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

The final model for estimating mean travel time to work includes log median income, percent of people that drove alone to work, percent of workers that took the bus, percent of workers that leave for work between 6-6:30 AM, categorical distance to the train station, and the number of Indego bike stations at the tract-level. The two features that lowered the RMSE the most were those that measured proximity to the train station, both the continuous distance and the categorically-defined distance substantially lowered CV RMSE by about .2. This was likely successful because areas within the ring are close to both West Philly and Center City which had larger negative residuals based on the original residual map. The initial idea was that this variable would account for individuals that commute out of the city for work. On the other hand, the most disappointing variable was the distance schools variable which increase the CV RMSE by only .01. Initially, I thought areas close to schools would have a higher mean commute time, however, this may not be a reliable assumption across the entire city if schools are evenly spatially distributed.
For the final model, I decided to use log median income as a variable to account for the skewed distribution of income groups. After the log transformation, the interpretation of this variable reads: a 1% increase in median income is associated with an increase of approximately .019 minutes in commute time to work. This relationship is statistically significant (p < .01).
Based on the final residual map, I would want to add a fixed effects term for individual neighborhoods across Philadelphia using the Philadelphia Neighborhoods shapefile from OpenDataPhilly. I think this would help mitigate the clustering of positive residuals in the Northwest and Northeast and clustering of negative residuals in Center City and West Philly. Again, although the magnitude of the residuals has decreased since running the first model, they still display an uneven distribution pattern.
The remaining error is likely driven due to statistical noise or uncertainty. The plot above shows that the most accurate estimates have a CV of less than 10%, with the most inaccurate estimates clustered between a CV of 10%-30%. Still, the tracts with the highest CV do not account for the greatest misses, so while statistical uncertainty plays a part, this relationship is not linear.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Getting started
Here, I am going to explore the claims that were made by this article stating that white poverty has exploded and that poverty rates have disproportionately spiked in certain neighborhoods in Philadelphia between 2010 and 2017. The article relies on data from the 2006-2010 and the 2013-2017 5-Year American Community Survey’s (ACS) to draw these conclusions. To investigate this claim, I will look at estimated impoverished individuals, impoverished white individuals, white population, total population, and median income to establish whether or not these claims are overstated or statistically sound.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Establishing neighborhoods
Specifically, the article makes the argument that the Eastwick neighborhood in Philadelphia has experienced the highest increase in poverty rate compared to the rest of the city between 2010 and 2017. The article also makes the argument that the Holmesburg neighborhood has experienced a large increase in white poverty rates, jumping from 2% to 19%. The last claim is that the Tioga neighborhood experienced the largest drop in median income in the city. The article does not specifically outline which Census tracts make up individual neighborhoods, so I am going to rely on the OpenDataPhilly Neighborhood designation to best approximate comparisons between neighborhoods. For areas with no recorded population (8 Census tracts), I will remove them from the data.


Show code
## Load neighborhoods shapefile ##
neighborhoods <- read_sf("data/philadelphia-neighborhoods")

# Join neighborhoods and census-tract data, assigning a tract to the neighborhood it shares the most overlap with #

# Ensure same coordinate system and transform if needed #

check_crs <- st_crs(neighborhoods)==st_crs(data2017)

neighborhoods <- st_transform(neighborhoods, st_crs(data2017))

neighborhoods <- st_make_valid(neighborhoods)

# Find the intersection between neighborhood and tract data #

neighborhoods_tracts2017 <- st_intersection(data2017, neighborhoods)

neighborhoods_tracts2010 <- st_intersection(data2010, neighborhoods)

# Assign tract to neighborhood they share most overlap with #

neighborhoods_tracts2017$area_overlap <- st_area(neighborhoods_tracts2017)

neighborhoods_tracts2010$area_overlap <- st_area(neighborhoods_tracts2010)

data2017 <- neighborhoods_tracts2017 %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  slice_max(area_overlap)

data2010 <- neighborhoods_tracts2010 %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  slice_max(area_overlap)

Analyzing poverty: Eastwick
First, I will look at how the poverty rate has changed between 2010 and 2017 in each neighborhood to determine if Eastwick experienced the highest increase in poverty rate.
There are 81 neighborhoods in Philadelphia that display having statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates from zero at a 90% confidence interval, whereas the remaining 58 neighborhoods did not display a statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates. This means that any observed change in poverty rates in those 58 neighborhoods could be due to sampling noise at a 90% confidence interval.

## Compute poverty rate across neighborhoods ##

              # there is no reported MOE for total population so I assume it is 0 #

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be. Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I am looking at the estimated number of individuals with bachelors degrees in all 14 counties across Massachusetts. Here, I will look at how counties of varying population sizes produce more or less reliable estimates of population characteristics, specifically the number of individuals with bachelors degrees. This analysis will shed light on how the surveys that rely on random samples to generalize population characteristics, like the American Community Survey, may inaccurately represent areas with smaller populations.

Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

The average population of high-confidence counties in Massachusetts is 675,837. The average population of low-confidence counties in Massachusetts is 20,751; however, it is worth nothing that only one county is considered in this average. This suggests that counties with higher populations have lower margins of error, producing more reliable estimates. At the county-level, due to the larger size of most counties, this is not a glaring issue in many cases. However, when working with more granular geographies (i.e., tract-level, block group-level), this effect can produce misleading estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Based on the analysis, the two counties we know the least about are Dukes County and Nantucket County. Interestingly enough, both counties are small island counties with active county governments, home to Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard.
The American Community Survey (ACS) works by targeting 3.5 million addresses annually as opposed to collecting data from all households in decade intervals like the Census. Because of this, the ACS relies on these samples to produce representative estimates at each geographic level, excluding block groups. The ACS has two survey versions: a one-year survey, which provides estimates for areas with at least 65,000 people, and a five-year survey, which provides estimates of all population-level areas. Because the ACS relies on a random sample of addresses to accurately estimate data points, smaller geographic areas receive less representation, making them more likely to have less representative estimates.
If a state agency were to view data across differently populated areas the same, this would result in less-populated, likely rural areas from receiving fair representation in receiving state resources. For example, if an agency were to rely on ACS estimates to fairly allocate housing funds to Scranton, with a population of around 75,000 people, vs. Wellsboro, with a population of 3,472 people, an area like Wellsboro would like receive more variable/inconsistent funding compared to an area like Scranton with a larger population.

To calculate the confidence levels, I adjusted the threshold for what is considered high confidence to be slightly more flexible, since tracts are a smaller geographic area than counties and inherently require a bit more flexibility.Thus, tracts with high confidence level have a margin of error percent less than 20%, tracts with a moderate confidence level have a margin of error percent between 20% and 30%, and tracts with a low confidence level have a margin of error percent greater then 30%. This supplemental analysis provides evidence that discrepancies in population even at a smaller scale can yield even bigger disparities in estimates. text:
Key Concepts
Localized Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) LISA refers to the spatial statistics used to measure the degree of spatial autocorrelation and clustering around individual locations on map. Clusters of high-high (individual-cluster) and low-low (individual-cluster) suggests that there is a pocket of space the model under or overestimates. If there are clusters of high-low or low-high, then that suggests that there are individual outliers within the clusters.
Contiguity Matrices Queen contiguity refers to any polygons that border each other, either directly or across. Rook contiguity refers to any polygons that directly borders another.

title: Week 3: ggplot and data viz
text:
Key Concepts
Different types of ggplots
If I want to know how a variable is spread… use geom_histogram()

If I want to know how two variables relate… use geom_point()

If I want to see how two groups compare… use geom_boxplot() or geom_col()

If I want to see how things change over time… use geom_line()

If I want to see how uncertain a value is… use geom_errorbar()

If I want to see multiple plots for different categories… use facet_wrap(~variable)

Statistics terms
Coefficient of Variation (CV) is the relative measure of sampling error. The standard error tells us how confident we can be that an estimate is reflective of the true population. For the Census Bureau, a low confidence interval is around 15% (high reliability), medium confidence interval is around 15%-30%, and a high confidence interval is 30% or above (high sampling error).
Derived Uncertainty - moe_sum() // adding estimates together - moe_prop() // one estimate as a share of another - moe_ratio() // one not a subset of another
The standard error of difference is sqrt(se1^2 + se2^2).
